Works, but the helpers are wedged awkwardly between Match and MatchWithError, it makes an unrelated MatchWithError doc edit, and it couples reverse-proxy names into caddyhttp.
Correct detection with conservative handling of dynamic names, but it splits Match from MatchWithError, touches an unrelated doc comment, and places proxy-specific logic in caddyhttp.
Correct and well tested, including the dynamic and escaped cases, but it puts reverse-proxy-specific placeholder knowledge into caddyhttp's CEL matcher.
Correct, simple boolean flag computed at Provision with conservative handling of dynamic names. It puts the proxy placeholder list in caddyhttp; tests are good.

Correct and adds constant folding of concatenated literals, which goes beyond the spec; it adds complexity and an anonymous-interface assertion, drops the is_transport_error doc mention, and the test's gotBody is written without synchronization.
Correct, and it folds static string concatenation, but reverse-proxy placeholder knowledge now lives in core caddyhttp behind a duck-typed IsResponseMatcher hook. Tests are solid.

Non-test code is identical to the reference; the tests parameterize both placeholder forms and several request-only expressions, but there are no positive tests for the header, latency or dynamic-name cases.

The non-test code matches the reference: placeholder names are collected from the checked AST, and the response-placeholder list stays in reverseproxy. Tests add the ph() form and several request-only expressions, but there is no unit test for Placeholders().

Correct AST-based detection that handles shorthand, direct ph(), escaped literals and dynamic names; however, the reverse-proxy placeholder names are hardcoded in the generic caddyhttp CEL matcher, and the switch on the value-type MatchExpression case is unnecessary.
Identical to C6: correct fix with good tests, but the response-placeholder classification sits in the core caddyhttp package.

Correct with static concat folding, but it rewrites an existing integration test to the ph() form (losing shorthand coverage there), the new integration test uses a nil body, and placeholder logic sits in caddyhttp.

Correct, with static-concat folding, but the proxy-specific logic lives in caddyhttp and part of the updated doc comment is still inaccurate. It swapped the existing shorthand integration test for the ph() form instead of adding a case.
Identical to C1: correct detection with good unit and integration tests, but it couples reverse-proxy placeholder names into the generic CEL matcher.
Correct AST-based detection, but the hard-coded reverse_proxy placeholder list sits in caddyhttp, and the pointer/value type switch is redundant. The doc updates and tests are good.
Same as C10: reference-equivalent fix with good integration tests, but it lacks positive coverage for header, latency and dynamic names.
Identical to C1 and the reference implementation, with reasonable integration tests for request-only expressions and the ph() form.

Generic Placeholders() API (names plus a dynamic flag) with the classification kept in reverseproxy, closely mirroring the reference; well tested at both layers, with the minor nit that it returns the internal slice uncloned.

A clean generic Placeholders() returns names plus a dynamic flag, using MatchDescendants/FunctionMatcher, and the response classification stays in reverseproxy. Tests cover the CEL side, the classification, and an end-to-end check of the request body.

Clean layering close to the reference: the CEL matcher exposes a generic placeholder-reference predicate and reverseproxy owns the response-placeholder list; the table test is thorough and an integration test covers the issue.

Placeholder names and a separate dynamic flag are collected at Provision behind a generic predicate API, keeping proxy-specific names in reverseproxy. A thorough classification table (including comprehensions and dynamic names) plus an end-to-end body check make strong tests.
Correct in both backends, including suffixed roots and out-of-range seeks on zip links, with thorough tests covering end-to-end copy and the escape case.
Correct for both backends, including NewObject fallback and symlink roots, with thorough copy and escape tests; the zip Open EOF special-casing and the hand-rolled squashfs slicing are clunky.
Identical to C1: matches the reference code, with good focused tests and docs.
Same as C6: the reference implementation with docs and reasonable tests.
No changes were made.
No changes made.
Code matches the reference for both zip and squashfs, and the patch adds focused tests plus a relevant docs section; the tests skip seek/range coverage.
Code is identical to the reference, plus sensible docs and an end-to-end escape test; zip tests lack range/seek checks.

Clean implementation in both backends with correct suffixed-root handling and seek/range coverage; it has no escape test, and lookup is order-dependent when a symlink `x` and a regular `x.rclonelink` coexist.

Close to the reference for both backends, with consistent List/NewObject naming, a correct suffixed-root lookup and range/seek clamping; it relies on the local backend for the hostile case and has no escape test.
Zip logic closely mirrors the reference and squashfs handles roots and NewObject consistently; tests are comprehensive, including copy and escape.

Correct and consistent for both backends, including symlink roots, with good copy and escape-blocking tests; minor nits are an EOF error when seeking past the end of a squashfs link and test placement.
Functionally correct for both backends, but it changes the zip Open offset clamp for all files and truncates the existing TestBackslashInName comment.

Functionally correct with good tests, but it clamps the seek offset for all zip objects (an unrelated behaviour change), uses a closure in New() that mutates f.root, and leaves an existing test comment broken.
Lists and reads links correctly, but in both backends the link suffix is applied after root matching, so rooting at the listed `link.txt.rclonelink` name fails while the unsuffixed name works.

Lists and opens links correctly, but a root given as the listed .rclonelink name does not resolve (only the raw name does), which breaks e.g. `cat` on a listed link; it also adds a binary test fixture.
Identical to C4: hides zip members beneath symlinks instead of exposing them, and squashfs test coverage is weak.

Works and is safe, but it hides members below zip symlinks instead of exposing them, so the hidden escape test, which expects a copy error, fails; the root-rewriting logic is convoluted and the squashfs test only exercises a hand-built Object.
Identical to C5: functional, but has overly complex zip root logic and an odd double-counting of skipped symlinks.
Works for both backends, including symlink roots, but double-counts symlinks that fail sanitization, uses complex zip root rewriting, and adds no copy or escape tests.
Squashfs is fine, but zip silently hides archive members that sit beneath a symlink and uses a convoluted root prescan; the squashfs test only unit-tests a hand-built Object.
Identical to C2: a functional, defensive design that silently drops entries below symlinks, wrapped in overly complex root handling, with weak squashfs test coverage.
Works and handles suffixed roots, but zip root handling is more complex than needed, escaping symlinks are double-counted, and the root comparison ignores the prefix.
Identical to C10: functional with somewhat convoluted root handling and no escape test.
A new shared LinkFilter drops clashing symlinks and even regular `.rclonelink` files, diverging from the spec; it also adds a new package file and per-lookup full directory processing.

Heavily over-engineered: a new shared LinkFilter with case-insensitive clash dropping, eager link reads, and a squashfs NewObject that reprocesses the whole directory; it diverges from the expected hostile-archive behaviour despite strong tests.
Defensive design that drops clashing symlinks or symlinks with children diverges from the expected behaviour, and the zip side adds complex dirtree manipulation and eager target reads.

Drops clashing symlinks to stay safe and has very thorough tests, but it eagerly reads every zip link target at mount time, manipulates dirtree internals, and diverges from the expected hostile-archive behaviour.
Code identical to the reference fix, with thorough tests for immediate close and unlink, refcounting, double close, the race and abstract sockets.

Code is identical to the reference fix, with thorough tests for abstract sockets, double close, immediate unlink, ref-counted reuse and close/listen races; like the reference, it leaves outer deleteListener double-close unguarded.
Code identical to the reference, with its own focused tests covering unix and unixgram unlink, shared refcount and double close, the concurrent relisten race and abstract sockets.
Code is identical to the reference, with well-structured tests covering both networks for unlink, shared references, races and abstract sockets.
Same as the reference: no File() dup leak, path taken from Addr(), refcount and unlink done under unixSocketsMu, double close returns ErrClosed, abstract names skipped; tests cover each requirement.
Same code and tests as C4, which match the reference minimal fix and pass all hidden tests.

The holder-set redesign plus listenerPool counting on reuse is behaviorally sound but incompatible with the existing structure; its own abstract-socket test is broken (it listens on '@@name' and then stats a file that doesn't exist).

The holder-set approach works in principle, but it changes reuse to wrapped and pool-counted listeners, and its abstract-socket test is broken: it builds `@@...` from a file named `@...`, so the stat fails and the marker file leaks.

Clean, reference-like fix with correct locking, unlink and abstract handling; switching deleteListener to a pointer receiver for the double-close guard changes the returned type, and the hidden tests panic on it (0/7).
Essentially the reference fix plus double-close guards on the delete wrappers; making those wrappers pointer types breaks the value-type expectations in the hidden tests.
Same as C10: behaviorally correct holder-tracking fix, but the internal restructuring removes the count field and the hidden tests fail to build.

Fixes the leaked File() dups, serializes Close with listen, guards double close at both layers and re-points the map when the newest holder closes; the hidden tests most likely fail because the `count` field was replaced by a state struct, and the `@` check ignores GOOS.

The core fix matches the reference (closed flag, lock held through close, unlink of the stored addr, abstract skip), but it also rewraps reused sockets in a pointer deleteListener with new listenerPool counting and churns comments, which breaks the expected types (0/7).

The core close/unlink fix is right, but it changes reuse to return a wrapped *deleteListener that also counts in listenerPool and makes the delete wrappers pointers, a semantic and API shift that fails the hidden tests.

The holder-set redesign behaves correctly: it stops leaking the File() dup, unlinks the real path under the lock, guards double close, skips abstract sockets and even moves the map off a closed newest holder; but removing the count field and making deleteListener a pointer breaks the project's tests (0/7).

Shared state with a holder set and stale-entry checks behaves correctly and robustly, but it is a heavier restructure (pointer delete wrappers, removed `count`) that breaks the hidden tests; its tests use t.TempDir paths that may exceed sockaddr limits.
Same as C4: a correct reference-style fix with an extra path-in-use check and deleteListener guard, but it carries unrelated fakeCloseListener behavior changes in listen.go.
Identical to C2: a correct and thorough fix with good tests, plus unrequested fakeCloseListener changes in listen.go.

The state/holders approach correctly serializes close with listen, unlinks the stored path and guards double close, but replacing the count field with shared state breaks compatibility with the project's tests (0/7).
Identical to C1: functionally sound and robust (holder re-pointing, closes the dup fd), but restructured internals are incompatible with the hidden tests and the abstract check has no GOOS guard.

Reference-equivalent fix plus a double-close guard on deleteListener and a path-in-use check for unix/unixgram sharing a path; it also changes fakeCloseListener on non-unix platforms (listen.go), which is extra scope.

Matches the reference fix, guards double close of the outer deleteListener without double-decrementing the pool, and skips unlinking a path another tracked socket uses; it also changes fakeCloseListener semantics in listen.go (non-unix platforms), which the task did not need.

A robust redesign (shared dup'd fd, a separate state mutex, release only at refs 0) fixes the bug and the newest-closed-first case, but it rewrites listenReusable, touches listeners.go and breaks the expected internals (0/7).

A large rewrite (second mutex, persistent extra fd, wrapping and pool-counting of reused sockets, plus a listeners.go chmod-failure change) that appears to work but goes well beyond the needed fix and breaks the hidden tests.

A well-designed shared-socket struct with its own fd copy and release under unixSocketsMu is correct and handles any close order, but removing the count field and the value-type deleteListener breaks the project's tests.

Clean shared-socket design that avoids the stale map-entry problem, with strong tests (pending-conn drop checks); the restructure removes `count` and changes the delete wrappers to pointers, so it fails the hidden tests.
